newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German jobless surges to new post-war record.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German jobless surges to new post-war record.

text.p: German unemployment surged by over a half a million to a new post-war record of 4.66 million in January, reaching levels last seen in the depths of the Great Depression of the 1930s.

The massive rise, due in part to harsh weather that saw large numbers of construction workers laid off, raised concern about the country's sputtering economic recovery and Bonn's ability to meet European monetary union requirements.
It also dashed many economists' hopes that unemployment would fall later this year and sharpened pressure on the Bundesbank to cut interest rates.
"January's unemployment numbers are truly hideous," said HSBC James Capel analyst Stephen King in London.
The unemployment rate, which is based on unadjusted data, rose to 12.2 percent, compared with 10.8 percent in December, the Federal Labour Office said on Thursday.

On a seasonally adjusted basis the number of unemployed workers rose by 160,000 from December to 4.317 million in January, or 11.3 percent of the workforce, smashing the consensus view among economists of a 52,000 rise.
As a result, Bonn will face higher dole costs than it had planned for in a budget tightened to meet EMU requirements, economists said.
"There is a high risk Germany will not meet the three percent gross domestic product-to-defict ratio target," Joerg Kraemer, a Merrill Lynch economist in Frankfurt, told Reuters.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bid to cut the defict to 2.9 percent of GDP assumes stable unemployment in 1997. Economists at Trinkaus Capital Management said that view was "no longer tenable" and raises "uncertainty and speculation about the stability of the government".
But Labour Office chief Bernhard Jagoda predicted more Germans would get back to work when the weather improves.

"This figure cannot be made to look good, but it should also be recognised that the situation in January contains seasonal unemployment, and it follows that in spring we can reckon with a clear reduction," Jagoda told reporters.

A Labour Office official said he expected unemployment to average between 4.1 million and 4.2 million this year, but admitted the number could rise if 1997 economic growth falls below Bonn's projection of 2.5 percent.

Bonn's labour outlook "is based on Germany experiencing relatively strong economic growth," said Eugen Spitznagel, a Labour Office research official. "If growth stagnates, the situation could be more serious."
"Looking at economic factors in the core areas of the economy, like manufacturing and building, there seems no prospect of a short-term upturn," he added.
Few economists said unemployment was likely to fall either.

"We are sticking to our forecast of 2.4 percent GDP growth," said King, the James Capel economist. "But regardless of the growth rate, companies will look to lower their labour costs in coming quarters. Unemploymnet will continue to rise."
Armin Kayser at SBC Warburg added that "Germany currently lacks the growth momentum which is necessary to stabilise the labour market."

Almost all of the economists said the Bundesbank would come under increasing pressure to cut interest rates to lift the economy, but the powerful central bank left rates unchanged at a council meeting on Thursday.
"Rates should go lower," said Nick Stamenkovic of DKB International in London.
In western Germany, the number of people out of work on a seasonally adjusted basis rose to 3.029 million in January, or 9.8 percent of the workforce from 2.951 million in December.
In eastern Germany, the number rose on an adjusted basis to 1.288 million from 1.207 million in December. The January adjusted employment rate was 17.3 percent.
